name: Botox alternatives (Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify)

lead: Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify and Letybo are botulinum toxin type A products used to soften frown lines in the same way as Botox. They come from different makers and are approved at different times, from Jeuveau in 2019 to Letybo in 2024.
Results typically last a few months. Brands differ in onset, spread and dosing units, and most published trials are in medical conditions rather than cosmetic comparisons.

paras: Each product blocks the nerve signal to a treated muscle, so it relaxes for a period of months. Differences between brands lie in the formulation and units, which are not interchangeable.

Reported effects include bruising, headache, drooping lids or brows and, rarely, spread of toxin (boxed warning). Antibodies can develop and reduce response. All are prescription products given by clinicians.

lead: Several botulinum toxin type A products compete with Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA) for cosmetic use, mainly treatment of glabellar (frown) lines. They include Dysport (abobotulinumtoxinA, sold in some markets as Azzalure), Xeomin (incobotulinumtoxinA, Bocouture), Jeuveau (prabotulinumtoxinA, Nuceiva), Daxxify (daxibotulinumtoxinA) and Letybo (letibotulinumtoxinA).[1][2]

All act by temporarily relaxing treated muscles. They are separate biological products whose units are not interchangeable, which is why the FDA gave them distinct nonproprietary names.[1] Typical cosmetic results last about three to four months, with some products reported to last longer.[1][2]
Most published trials of these products involve medical conditions such as cervical dystonia and limb spasticity; cosmetic registrations include comparisons in glabellar lines.

paras: Dysport is described as acting somewhat faster than Botox in some accounts, with more spread from the injection site, and a rough conversion of 2.5 to 3 Dysport units to 1 Botox unit is cited, although units are product-specific.[2] A double-blind study in cervical dystonia tested a three-to-one ratio of Dysport to Botox units, and a later crossover study examined the products' relative potencies.[3][4]

Jeuveau was approved in the US in February 2019 for glabellar lines.[2] Daxxify was approved in September 2022 and Letybo in February 2024, each for glabellar lines on the basis of pivotal trials; the most common adverse events listed for them include headache, eyelid drooping and facial muscle weakness.[1] Xeomin is named as a cosmetic neuromodulator, though the references reviewed give no cosmetic approval date for it.[2]

Adverse effects of botulinum toxins in cosmetic use include bruising, headache, flu-like symptoms, partial facial weakness and eyelid or brow drooping; spread of toxin from the injection site led the FDA to add boxed warnings in 2009.[1] Antibodies that neutralize the toxin develop in a substantial number of patients receiving muscle-relaxant treatment according to an older laboratory study, and the authors noted this often necessitated ending treatment.[5] Descriptions of cosmetic use say repeated treatment can shorten results or cause non-response.[2]

Studies of these products are mostly in medical conditions. Randomised trials of Dysport covered upper-limb spasticity after stroke, hip adductor spasticity in multiple sclerosis and cervical dystonia.[6][7][8] Registered cosmetic trials include a non-inferiority trial of another abobotulinumtoxinA product against Dysport in glabellar lines (n=146), a trial of different injection volumes of Azzalure in glabellar lines (n=62), and studies comparing the muscle activity or field of effect of two commercial toxin preparations in wrinkles.[9][10][11][12] Published head-to-head cosmetic outcomes between all brands are limited in the sources reviewed.
